title: Control Charts for Multi-Agent Systems
claim: Agents with fixed memory stop adapting to a changing environment, while agents with updating memory keep tracking it.
layout: 3 columns, 2 stacked rows in left and middle, static vs dynamic colors
description: Six line plots in three columns on a white background, each with a light grid. The left column has two stacked panels titled Static Memory and Dynamic Memory: Agent Positions. Both show TDKPS position against iteration for five colored agents. In the static panel the agents rise quickly and then flatten. In the dynamic panel they keep fluctuating. The middle column has two stacked panels of mean accuracy against iteration. The first is for non-temporal questions, where static and dynamic both sit near 1.0. The second is for temporal questions, where static (orange) collapses to about 0.2 and dynamic (blue) stays around 0.4 to 0.7. The right column is one tall panel, Isomirror: Static vs Dynamic. It shows both curves dropping sharply from 1.0. The static curve then stays near zero while the dynamic curve keeps fluctuating at higher values. Orange marks static and blue marks dynamic.
caption: Static ($\rho = 0$) vs.\ dynamic ($\rho = 0.05$) memory. Left: TDKPS embeddings $\psi_n^{(t)}$ for individual agents. Middle: Mean accuracy on static and environmental queries. Right: Iso-mirror trajectories $\phi^{(t)}$. Dynamic memory is necessary for agents to adapt to a dynamic environment.
abstract: Generative agents have proven to be powerful assistants in a wide variety of contexts. Given this success, users are now deploying agents with minimal restrictions in open ended, multi-agent environments. Current methods for monitoring the dynamics of open-ended multi-agent systems are limited to aggregate statistics, qualitative inspection, or detecting change between two fixed timepoints. In this paper, we extend the process-theoretic notion of adaptive control charts to multi-agent systems to enable automated monitoring. Using simulation, we demonstrate that adaptive control charts are necessary for monitoring multi-agent systems that can learn from their environment. We further demonstrate, both empirically and theoretically, that adaptive control charts are susceptible to adversarial agents that defect sufficiently slowly. These results suggest a fundamental tradeoff in multi-agent system control: monitors with fixed baselines flag legitimate learning, while monitors with adaptive baselines admit slow adversaries. We conjecture this holds for any monitor.
